items.title: Gen Z is getting nostalgic for the Obama era — with an asterisk
items.summary:
“Millennial optimism exists because Obama won elections so decisively that they had time to hit the club afterward,” Olivia Julianna, a Democratic strategist and content creator, said. | Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images 

Millennial optimism is making a comeback online, thanks to the Democrats’ blue tsunami in this month’s midterm election. Social media is filled with videos, songs, and edits celebrating the midterms and linking the feeling to Barack Obama’s victories and the various cultural signifiers of the time, from indie bands to “ girlboss” CEOs . Many of them are produced by Gen Z users who have little memory of the era themselves. 

To some left-leaning millennials, it’s a teachable moment. On Instagram the day after the election, 37-year-old Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) gave her younger followers a lesson in the roots of “millennial cringe,” that mix of hope and earnestness that Gen Zers often see as cloying and naive.

“Imagine all the seats we flipped last night, that feeling, plus on top of it, electing the first Black president ever. And on top of that, you did it the first time you ever voted? That hits generationally ,” Ocasio-Cortez said . “Like, you are chasing that feeling ever since. And because you did it the first time you ever voted, you’re like, ‘Yeah, we can change the world. Yeah, why not. We did it the first time. Why not just do it again?’”

But while some millennials (including many of the victorious candidates ) might proudly claim this moment as a restoration of their culture — everyone back to Hamilton ! — some of the Gen…
items.t: Gen Z is getting nostalgic for the Obama era — with an asterisk

items.title: How Uruguay built a national care system from the ground up
items.summary:
Imagine a family with two working parents who can drop off their 2-year-old at a neighborhood childcare center for the workday for little to no fee. Their 4-year-old goes to a free public preschool nearby. Across town, the mother’s 82-year-old father, who can no longer bathe or dress himself, is visited by a personal assistant the government mostly pays for, 80 hours a month.

It’s not a daydream, it’s just a normal day for many families in Uruguay. 

And it is not just for lower-income households. A little more than a decade ago, Uruguay passed a law declaring that care for children, seniors, people with disabilities, and caregivers themselves is a right, and has been working to make good on that promise ever since. The resulting National Integrated Care System, known as SNIC (Sistema Nacional Integrado de Cuidados), has become a model around the world for treating care not as a privilege but as public infrastructure.

Across the country of about 3.4 million people, the system now provides early childhood care for some 78,000 children , subsidized home assistants for more than 6,000 people with severe disabilities, and day centers and emergency call services for older adults — through a network of community-run childcare centers, certified care workers, and a national agency that coordinates it all.

The undertaking has been huge, and the buildout is still in process. But the reasons for it echo across other high-income countries right now, including the United States, namely: falling birth rates, an aging population, and generations of women who are no longer willing or…
items.t: How Uruguay built a national care system from the ground up

items.title: Can depression really become dazzling dance? The biggest ever BalletBoyz show is a huge feat
items.summary:
Sadler’s Wells, London
In Six Lethargies, Iván Pérez and Seirian Griffiths have devised a mammoth production of aching, ethereal sadness

‘If I write what I feel, will you feel it, too?” That was the question behind singer-songwriter turned composer Keaton Henson’s Six Lethargies. Perhaps that is every artist’s mission, but for Henson it was specifically his experiences with anxiety and depression that he wanted to translate into music. Now it has been turned into dance by the BalletBoyz. If they dance it, will we feel it?

Six Lethargies is the largest production in the 25-year history of the BalletBoyz. Once just two ex-Royal Ballet dancers, Michael Nunn and William Trevitt, this iteration is a company of 44 dancers (male and female), a 37-piece string orchestra, and not one but two choreographers working together: former Dance Theatre Heidelberg artistic director Iván Pérez and talented newcomer Seirian Griffiths.

items.title: ‘I was drinking at 15, going to parties, being groomed and abused’: the grim reality of age-gap relationships
items.summary:
Do teenagers need more protection from predatory adults? As campaigners in the UK call for changes to the law on consent, we talk to five people who became entangled with much older men and women

In the wake of the allegations against David Walliams (which he denies) – that he wooed young fans with promises of professional help – there have been renewed calls for a staggered age of consent. Sometimes called Romeo and Juliet laws, rules already exist in some US states, Canada and France to prevent “age-gap relationships” or, to put it another way, the sexual exploitation of teenagers by adults. The suggestion from UK campaigners Close the Consent Gap is for it to be illegal to have an age gap of more than three years if anyone is under 18, and last week, Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, called for “serious conversations” on the potential for legislative change.

I have spoken to people in their 40s, 50s, 60s and 70s, describing age gaps far greater than three years; often with people twice their age or more. It’s noticeable that social norms and taboos didn’t change hugely between the start of the 1960s and the end of the 80s; in most cases, their parents didn’t bat an eyelid and teachers, if they were aware, didn’t intervene. But the more striking through-line, from the 60s to the 00s, is how these…

items.summary:
From left, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and President Donald Trump take part in a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China. | Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

President Donald Trump is on his way back from China after a four-day Asia trip that included taking in a surreal cover of “Y.M.C.A.,” heaping praise on a noted kleptocrat, and making earnest — if slightly cringe! — declarations of star-crossed presidential friendship . 

But the highlight of the trip was surely Trump’s unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the first between those countries’ leaders. 

The three men sat around a comically large and reflective roundtable to discuss issues like reforming the United Nations, increasing the world’s supply of petroleum, and reducing the risk of nuclear war, which they all thankfully agree would be a bad idea.

A major nuclear treaty between the US and Russia lapsed nine months ago , and China has been a sticking point to negotiating a new one. In fact, all three countries are — in one realm or another — major obstacles to each other’s geopolitical ambitions. 

Accordingly, no breakthroughs were reached during their hour-long chat. But they did agree to keep chatting…including about nuclear proliferation.

items.title: The astonishing toll of America’s food stamp cuts
items.summary:
A child helps load boxes at a California food bank in January 2026.  | Paul Bersebach/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images 

As we head into Thanksgiving, a holiday dedicated to abundance and sharing, millions of Americans are struggling to afford groceries. Children, in particular, are at risk, their parents forced to choose between listening to their baby cry because they’re hungry or watch them shiver because they can’t pay for heating as the weather turns cold.

Many of us have felt the costs of everyday life getting steeper, squeezing people at the gas pump and the grocery store. But some folks are facing not only inflation but the loss of government benefits: Federal assistance for food has been drying up since the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last year. According to the estimates from the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, about 5.5 million people have fallen off of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (or SNAP) between the law’s passage in July 2025 and July 2026 — a 13 percent decline in just one year. About 2 million of the people who lost benefits are children. At this point, SNAP participation has reached a 17-year low, the lowest it’s been since the Great Recession, and not because people don’t need it.

View Link 
 It is as acute of an affordability crisis as any that Americans are facing right now. Nearly 1 in 4 US adults experienced food insecurity in 2025, according to the Urban Institute ; 8 percent said in a recent federal survey that their household often or sometimes did not have enough to…
items.t: The astonishing toll of America’s food stamp cuts

items.title: Come to GTA VI for the crime spree. Stay for the manatee.
items.summary:
In Grand Theft Auto IV, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades. | Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive 

There are plenty of reasons to be excited for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, which came out today. There are the heists, the incredibly realistic depictions of Florida , the surprisingly deep romance , and, you know, the car theft. It’s been 13 years since the last installment of the incredibly popular game series — basically an eternity in 2026 terms.

But personally, I’m interested in the pelicans in flight at sunset and the green scales of an iguana in the street, as seen in the game’s second trailer . There are more than 170 animals in the game, like alligators, manatees, and frogs. There are also 62 species of birds, and players can pull out binoculars and record them all in a logbook. 

Now I’m not a video game writer. I write about biodiversity. So this stuff is basically catnip for me, and I’m not the only one. There are Reddit threads full of excited birdwatchers who are saying that crime sprees will come second to birding in the new game, or that they want to get one of the game’s protagonists, Lucia, some cute birding outfits. The top comment in the New York Times’s review of the game says, “my roommate gets to play the actual game. I get to find all 67 [sic] species of birds. Truly a game for everyone.”

While most of the game takes place in Vice City, which is developer Rockstar’s take on Miami, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades and…
items.t: Come to GTA VI for the crime spree. Stay for the manatee.

items.title: Do you feel like you can’t afford to have kids? This might be why.
items.summary:
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) speaks during a news conference on the Family and Medical Leave Act at the US Capitol on February 1, 2023. | Alex Wong/Getty Images 

When it comes to wanting kids, the size of your paycheck seems to matter less than which way it’s moving.

That’s one of the key findings in the 2026 American Family Survey, released Thursday by the Wheatley Institute at Brigham Young University and the Deseret News, which has been conducted annually since 2015. This year’s survey was conducted by YouGov among 3,000 Americans, along with an additional 1,500 adults ages 18 to 40. 

Among childless adults under 50, 44 percent of those whose finances improved over the past year said they definitely want children, compared with 24 percent of those whose finances got worse. Income made much less of a difference: 29 percent of those earning under $50,000 said they definitely want kids, compared with 32 percent of those earning $100,000 or more.

“Whether your finances are going up or down tells people more about the future than does your income now,” said Andrew Cherlin, a professor emeritus of sociology at Johns Hopkins University who studies family formation and wasn’t involved in the survey.

View Link 
 Young adults were also more likely than older Americans to say they need certain things in place before having a baby, like financial stability, an established career, or a house. Higher earners named even more conditions.

items.t: What makes Americans feel financially ready to have kids? It’s complicated.

items.title: What does America get from the blue wave? It depends who wins this crucial argument.
items.summary:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) poses for a photo with newly elected Democratic senators in his office in the US Capitol Building on November 9, 2026, in Washington, DC. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty 

When a party loses badly in an election cycle, what typically ensues is a frenzy of finger-pointing as different voices and factions advance their theory of what went wrong.

In the wake of the 2026 blue tsunami, Democrats have a happier problem: They get to argue over who gets most credit for this smashing win.

Indeed, prominent members of the two main sides in the party’s long-simmering civil war — progressives and moderates — barely paused to take a breath before arguing that the results precisely vindicated their theories of what American voters want, what makes for effective politics, and where the Democratic Party should go.

Key takeaways 

Moderates point out that most Democrats who flipped key Senate states distanced themselves from progressives and the left on some issues, and argue that more solidly progressive candidates won by less impressive margins. 

Progressives point out that winning Democratic candidates, even in red states, embraced the rhetoric of economic populism, criticizing billionaires and corporations. 

Progressives argue that only major structural reforms to the economy can satisfy voters; moderates are urging a more limited focus on the cost of living. 

Democratic leaders will have to decide whose case is more persuasive as they shape the party’s governing agenda. 

The progressives say that winning candidates broadly ran on bold…
items.t: Democrats won big. Now they’re arguing about why.

items.title: How Nvidia’s chaos trickles down to you
items.summary:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sits for an interview with Bloomberg News in London on October 14, 2026. | Bloomberg via Getty Images 

If you didn’t know a lot about Nvidia a month ago, what you know now is salacious, essential, and probably a little bit misleading. 

The multitrillion-dollar chipmaker has primarily been in the news because its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang had a few affairs — one with a possible spy — and resigned. This has been a huge story, not just because of the sex scandal but also because Nvidia has been propping up the entire AI industry, as its primary chip supplier and frequent financier, and, by proxy, propping up the global economy.

The downside risk is almost catastrophic: If Huang brings Nvidia down with him, the whole economic house of cards could collapse .

Don’t freak out. This probably won’t happen. Nvidia just reported its third-quarter earnings and beat estimates , seemingly setting up interim CEO Colette Kress for success (even if it ultimately disappointed Wall Street ). The company’s board also declared that it would not reinstate Huang , despite Huang’s very public willingness to be reinstated . So the company isn’t exactly in crisis mode.

That doesn’t mean it will avoid a reckoning, But the reckoning is much broader than the Huang storyline — and if it comes, might even be beneficial.

Nvidia is facing a raft of investigations and potential new regulations as a more AI-skeptical Congress prepares to take power , not to mention growing competition from tech giants, like Google , that have started making their own highly…
items.t: How Nvidia’s chaos trickles down to you

items.title: Anthropic’s early birds are getting very rich
items.summary:
Anthropic signage at the Morgan Stanley headquarters in New York on November 18, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

Americans have debated, derided, praised, and protested the frontier AI labs. But they’ve never been able to directly own a piece of one…until tomorrow at 9 am.

That’s when Anthropic, developer of the chatbot Claude, is expected to go public at a valuation of more than $1 trillion . That would immediately rank the almost-six-year-old lab among the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies — up there with the likes of Walmart and JPMorgan Chase.

It’s a major public test of what investors think Anthropic is worth, at a moment when a lot of people — policymakers, regulators, and technologists among them — are questioning the economic and social value of the AI industry. AI stocks have been shaky lately, and many of the new congressional Democrats have promised to take a tougher stance toward data centers and related technology. 

But you wouldn’t know it from the hype around the IPO, which is on track to become one of the largest ever. Anthropic initially set a price range of $70 to $78 a share, then reportedly revised the offering at $83 per share as demand surged far beyond the number of shares available. 

Investors are apparently betting that Anthropic has more growing to do. For ordinary buyers, that represents a chance to share in a company whose technology could cost us our jobs…
items.t: Anthropic’s early birds are getting very rich

items.title: Trump’s looming nominations crunch
items.summary:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) in the US Capitol Building on November 10, 2026. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images 

This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .

Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is running out of time to get his nominees confirmed. 

What’s happening? On Wednesday, outgoing Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy blocked Trump’s nominee to lead the National Science Foundation, Jim O’Neill, from confirmation. And last night, the White House pulled another nominee, would-be FDA commissioner Heidi Overton, from consideration ahead of a Wednesday committee vote. 

Both come at the worst possible time for Trump, who’s facing a dwindling legislative calendar with a Republican Senate majority on its way out. 

Cassidy, a physician, chairs the Senate health committee, which is responsible for approving both nominations before they go to the full Senate. On Tuesday evening, he wrote in a social media post that “unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”

What’s the context? A new Congress will be sworn in on January 3, in about a month and a half, and Democrats will hold sizable majorities in both chambers.

In reality, though, the Senate has less time than that to deal with new nominations: Not only are the holidays approaching, but Congress has other big-ticket priorities on its plate, including heading off another government shutdown and potential deals on…
items.t: Trump’s looming nominations crunch

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning.

While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature.

items.title: Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era
items.summary:
James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

items.title: Eurovision Asia: a diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop
items.summary:
On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia.

Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia.

The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices.

Regional flavour

Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together).

While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English.

By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual.

items.t: Eurovision Asia: a diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop
